title: Ἁλιεὺς αὐλῶν
source: Émile Chambry, Ésope: Fables, texte établi et traduit (Les Belles Lettres, Paris, 1927), fable 24. Text as printed, including Chambry's editorial punctuation (« », ⟨ ⟩ for editorial supplements). Pronunciation: reconstructed Attic, after W. S. Allen, Vox Graeca. Romanization: standard classical transliteration (ē/ō; th/ph/ch; y for υ, u in diphthongs; h = rough breathing; ēi/āi/ōi for iota subscript; accents omitted).

sentences.t: Ἁλιεὺς αὐλητικῆς ἔμπειρος, ἀναλαβὼν αὐλοὺς καὶ τὰ δίκτυα, παρεγένετο εἰς τὴν θάλασσαν καὶ στὰς ἐπί τινος προβλῆτος πέτρας, τὸ μὲν πρῶτον ᾖδε, νομίζων αὐτομάτους πρὸς τὴν ἡδυφωνίαν τοὺς ἰχθύας ἐξαλεῖσθαι πρὸς αὐτόν.
sentences.tr: Halieus aulētikēs empeiros, analabōn aulous kai ta diktya, paregeneto eis tēn thalassan kai stas epi tinos problētos petras, to men prōton ēide, nomizōn automatous pros tēn hēdyphōnian tous ichthyas exaleisthai pros auton.
sentences.l: A fisherman skilled in the pipes, having taken up his pipes and his nets, came to the sea and, having stood on a jutting rock, at first sang, thinking that the fish would of their own accord leap out at the sweet sound toward him.
sentences.i: A fisherman who was a skilled piper took up his pipes and his nets, came down to the sea and, taking his stand on a jutting rock, played at first, supposing that the fish would leap out to him of their own accord at the sweetness of the sound.
sentences.n: αὐλητική (with τέχνη understood) is the art of the αὐλός — not a flute but a double-reed pipe, closer in sound to an oboe, and the ordinary instrument of Greek music. ἔμπειρος takes the genitive of what one is practised in. ᾖδε, imperfect of ἀείδω, is properly “sang”: Greek uses it of an instrument's voice as readily as of a singer's. αὐτομάτους is predicative, “of their own accord.”

sentences.t: Ὡς δὲ, αὐτοῦ ἐπὶ πολὺ διατεινομένου, οὐδὲν πέρας ἠνύετο, ἀποθέμενος τοὺς αὐλοὺς ἀνείλετο τὸ ἀμφίβληστρον καὶ βαλὼν κατὰ τοῦ ὕδατος πολλοὺς ἰχθύας ἤγρευσεν.
sentences.tr: Hōs de, autou epi poly diateinomenou, ouden peras ēnyeto, apothemenos tous aulous aneileto to amphiblēstron kai balōn kata tou hydatos pollous ichthyas ēgreusen.
sentences.l: But when, with him straining at it a long while, no end was being accomplished, having laid the pipes aside he took up his casting-net and, having thrown it down into the water, caught many fish.
sentences.i: But when, for all his long exertion, nothing came of it, he laid the pipes aside, took up his casting-net, threw it into the water and caught a great many fish.
sentences.n: αὐτοῦ … διατεινομένου is a genitive absolute, concessive here: “though he strained at it a long while.” ἐπὶ πολύ is “over a long stretch.” ἀμφίβληστρον is the round throwing-net, cast over the fish and drawn shut — a different tool from the σαγήνη of the fable before. κατά with the genitive is “down into.”

sentences.t: Ἐκβαλὼν δὲ αὐτοὺς ἀπὸ τοῦ δικτύου ἐπὶ τὴν ἠιόνα, ὡς ἐθεάσατο σπαίροντας, ἔφη· « Ὦ κάκιστα ζῷα, ὑμεῖς, ὅτε μὲν ηὔλουν, οὐκ ὠρχεῖσθε, νῦν δὲ, ὅτε πέπαυμαι, τοῦτο πράττετε. »
sentences.tr: Ekbalōn de autous apo tou diktyou epi tēn ēiona, hōs etheasato spairontas, ephē· « Ō kakista zōia, hymeis, hote men ēuloun, ouk ōrcheisthe, nyn de, hote pepaumai, touto prattete. »
sentences.l: And having thrown them out of the net onto the beach, when he saw them flapping, he said: « O most wretched creatures, you, when I was piping, would not dance, but now, when I have stopped, you do this. »
sentences.i: Throwing them out of the net onto the beach and seeing them flapping about, he said: « Miserable creatures — while I was piping you would not dance, and now that I have stopped, this is what you do. »
sentences.n: ὅτε μέν … νῦν δέ holds the two times apart, “then … but now.” The imperfects ηὔλουν and ὠρχεῖσθε cover the stretch of time; πέπαυμαι is a perfect, the state he stands in now, “I have done.” σπαίροντας, of fish, is the twitching of the landed catch — the dance he asked for, at the wrong moment.

sentences.t: Πρὸς τοὺς παρὰ καιρόν τι πράττοντας ὁ λόγος εὔκαιρος.
sentences.tr: Pros tous para kairon ti prattontas ho logos eukairos.
sentences.l: Against those who do anything out of season the story is well-timed.
sentences.i: The story suits those who do a thing at the wrong moment.
sentences.n: A second closing formula, terser than ὁ λόγος δηλοῖ: πρός with the accusative names whom the story is aimed at, and εὔκαιρος means “well-timed, apt.” The point is in the words themselves — a fable about doing things παρὰ καιρόν, out of season, is itself εὔκαιρος, in season.
